title: How Many Workdays Are in 2027? Month-by-Month Table and Holidays
meta: 2027 has 261 weekdays and 249 workdays after federal holidays, including Dec 31 for New Year 2028. Monthly table, quarters and PTO tips.
html:
There are 261 weekdays in 2027. Take out the 11 federal holidays, plus Friday, December 31, which is the observed day off for New Year's Day 2028, and you are left with 249 workdays on the federal holiday calendar. If your employer stays open on December 31, your count is 250.

That is 1,992 hours at 8 hours a day, 88 short of the 2,080-hour year most payroll departments assume.

The 2027 federal holidays and when they are observed

Federal holidays that land on a Saturday are observed on the Friday before, and holidays that land on a Sunday move to the Monday after. Four of them shift in 2027, and the New Year's rule pulls an extra day off into December 2027.

HolidayActual dateObserved (day off)
New Year's DayFri, Jan 1Same day
Birthday of Martin Luther King, Jr.Mon, Jan 18Same day
Washington's BirthdayMon, Feb 15Same day
Memorial DayMon, May 31Same day
JuneteenthSat, Jun 19Fri, Jun 18
Independence DaySun, Jul 4Mon, Jul 5
Labor DayMon, Sep 6Same day
Columbus DayMon, Oct 11Same day
Veterans DayThu, Nov 11Same day
Thanksgiving DayThu, Nov 25Same day
Christmas DaySat, Dec 25Fri, Dec 24
New Year's Day 2028Sat, Jan 1, 2028Fri, Dec 31

The last row is the one people miss: January 1, 2028 is a Saturday, so 2027 holds 12 observed holiday weekdays even though there are only 11 federal holidays.

Workdays in 2027, month by month

Weekdays are Monday through Friday. Workdays are weekdays minus the observed federal holidays in the table above. Hours assume an 8-hour day.

MonthWeekdaysHolidaysWorkdaysHours (8/day)
January21219152
February20119152
March23023184
April22022176

Total261122491,992

Workdays per quarter

  • Q1 (Jan to Mar): 61 workdays, 488 hours
  • Q2 (Apr to Jun): 63 workdays, 504 hours
  • Q3 (Jul to Sep): 64 workdays, 512 hours
  • Q4 (Oct to Dec): 61 workdays, 488 hours

Why 261 and not 260? 2027 has 52 full weeks plus one extra day, and that day is a Friday.

Why your own count may be different

Most private employers do not follow the federal calendar day for day. Adjust the 249 with this checklist:

  • Holidays you work. Many private employers stay open on Columbus Day, Veterans Day, Washington's Birthday or Juneteenth. Add one workday for each.
  • December 31. Plenty of companies treat New Year's Eve as a normal day. If yours does, add one.
  • Extra company holidays. The day after Thanksgiving (Nov 26) is a common addition. Subtract one for each extra day off.
  • Compressed schedules. On a four-day, 10-hour schedule you work fewer days but roughly the same hours, so count hours, not days.

A quick formula: 249 + federal holidays you work - extra company holidays off = your 2027 workdays.

Using the count to plan PTO

Several 2027 holidays sit next to a weekend or on a Thursday, so a few PTO days go a long way:

  • Juneteenth: observed Friday, June 18, giving a three-day weekend with no PTO.
  • Independence Day: observed Monday, July 5, giving another three-day weekend.
  • Veterans Day: Thursday, Nov 11. One PTO day on Friday, Nov 12 makes it four days off (if your employer observes it).
  • Thanksgiving: Thursday, Nov 25. One PTO day on Friday, Nov 26 makes it four days.
  • Year end: with Friday, Dec 24 and Friday, Dec 31 both observed, taking Dec 27 to Dec 30 (4 PTO days) gives 10 days off in a row, from Friday, Dec 24 through Sunday, Jan 2, 2028.

To check a stretch like that, or to count the days until a trip, use the Days Between Dates calculator.

Payroll: the 2,080-hour convention vs the real 2027 calendar

Payroll teams usually treat a full-time year as 2,080 hours (52 weeks x 40 hours), a convention rather than a count of any real year:

MeasureDaysHours
Payroll convention2602,080
All weekdays in 20272612,088
Workdays after 12 observed holidays2491,992
  • Salaried staff are paid the same annual salary whatever the calendar holds. The 2,080 figure is mainly used to translate salary into an hourly rate: $60,000 / 2,080 = about $28.85 an hour.
  • Hourly staff with paid holidays are paid for every weekday. At $25 an hour, 2,088 hours comes to $52,200, slightly more than the $52,000 the convention suggests.
  • Hourly staff without paid holidays are paid only for hours worked. At $25 an hour, 1,992 hours comes to $49,800.

Federal wage law does not require employers to pay for holidays you do not work, or to pay a premium just because you work on one, so holiday pay depends on your employer's policy. For tracking actual time on the clock, the Hours calculator adds up shifts and breaks.

Quick answers about the 2027 work calendar

Is December 31, 2027 a day off?
For federal employees, yes. It is the observed New Year's Day because January 1, 2028 falls on a Saturday. Private employers, banks and markets set their own schedules, so check with yours.

How many weekend days are in 2027?
104. The year has 365 days and 261 weekdays.

Is 2027 a leap year?
No. 2027 has 365 days. The next leap year is 2028.

Which month has the most workdays?
March, with 23 weekdays and no federal holidays. January and February are the shortest at 19 each.

Try it with your numbers: plug your own start and end dates into the Days Between Dates calculator, or total a week of shifts with the Hours calculator.

Sources

  • U.S. Office of Personnel Management – Federal holidays (dates and observed-day rules)
  • U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division: Overtime Pay

All dates, weekday counts and totals were computed day by day using the Saturday-to-Friday and Sunday-to-Monday observance rules. Last reviewed: November 2026. This is general information about the calendar; your employer's holiday schedule and pay policy decide your actual workdays and pay.

title: What a $1,000 Credit Card Balance Costs at 20%, 25% and 30% APR
meta: At 25% APR, paying $25 a month on $1,000 takes 87 months and $1,172 in interest. See 20%, 25% and 30% APR tables plus balance transfer math.
html:
A $1,000 credit card balance costs about $16.67 a month in interest at 20% APR, $20.83 at 25%, and $25.00 at 30%, before you pay down a single dollar of the balance. The total cost depends mostly on your payment: at 25% APR, paying $25 a month takes 87 months and $1,172 in interest, while paying $100 a month clears it in 12 months for $133.

At 30% APR, a $25 payment never pays the card off at all, because it only covers the interest.

The cost of $1,000 at three APRs and three payments

Each cell shows how many months it takes to reach zero and the total interest paid along the way. The figures assume no new purchases, no fees, a fixed monthly payment, and interest charged each month at the APR divided by 12.

APRInterest-only cost per monthPay $25/monthPay $50/monthPay $100/month
20%$16.6767 months, $661.7025 months, $226.6312 months, $103.06
25%$20.8387 months, $1,172.4327 months, $307.1012 months, $133.23
30%$25.00Never paid off29 months, $403.5812 months, $165.30

Three things stand out:

  • The payment matters more than the rate. Going from $25 to $50 a month at 20% APR cuts the interest from $661.70 to $226.63. Dropping the APR from 30% to 20% at $50 a month saves about $177.
  • Small payments stretch for years. At 25% APR, $25 a month means more than seven years of payments and more interest than the original balance.
  • Interest-only is a treadmill. If your payment is at or below the interest-only figure, the balance does not shrink. At 30% that line is exactly $25.

Your card's actual minimum payment is set by a formula in your cardholder agreement, and it usually falls as the balance falls, which makes payoff even slower than a fixed payment. Your monthly statement must show how long payoff would take at the minimum. To run your own balance, rate and payment, use the Credit Card Payoff calculator.

How card interest is actually charged

The table uses a simple monthly calculation so the numbers are easy to follow. Real cards usually work from your balance day by day:

  • The APR is converted to a daily periodic rate, typically the APR divided by 365 (some issuers use 360). At 25% APR that is about 0.0685% a day.
  • The issuer tracks your balance each day of the billing cycle, adding purchases and subtracting payments as they post, and usually averages those daily balances.
  • Interest is the average daily balance times the daily rate times the days in the cycle. For a steady $1,000 at 25% APR, that is about $0.685 a day, or roughly $20.55 in a 30-day cycle and $21.23 in a 31-day cycle.

Paying earlier in the cycle lowers your average balance and trims interest a little. Methods differ, so your cardholder agreement explains the exact one.

The grace period: how to pay zero interest

Most cards give you a grace period on purchases: if you pay the full statement balance by the due date, you are not charged interest on those purchases. Federal rules require the issuer to mail or deliver your bill at least 21 days before the payment is due.

The catch is that carrying any balance usually ends the grace period. Once you carry $1,000 over, new purchases typically start building interest right away, and you generally need to pay the balance in full, sometimes for more than one cycle, to get the grace period back. Cash advances usually have no grace period at all. Check your card's terms for the exact rules.

Worked case: is a balance transfer worth the fee?

A balance transfer moves the debt to a card with a low or 0% promotional rate, usually for a fee of a few percent of the amount moved. Fees of 3% to 5% are common, but check the offer. Here is the math on $1,000, assuming a 0% rate for 12 months and that you pay it off within the promotion:

OptionUpfront costMonthly paymentTotal cost of borrowing
Stay at 25% APR$0$85.84$157.53 interest (14 months)
Transfer with 3% fee$30$85.84$30.00 (12 months)
Transfer with 5% fee$50$87.50$50.00 (12 months)

The fee is added to the balance, so with a 3% fee you owe $1,030, and $1,030 / 12 = $85.84 a month (rounded up) clears it in time. Paying the same amount on the 25% card takes 14 months and costs $157.53 in interest, so the transfer saves about $128. The 5% version saves about $104 compared with paying $87.50 a month at 25%.

The savings shrink if you do not finish before the promotion ends, because any remaining balance moves to the regular APR. New purchases on the transfer card can also lose their grace period.

If the $1,000 card is one of several debts, the Debt Snowball vs Avalanche calculator shows whether to aim extra payments at the smallest balance or the highest rate first.

What people ask about a $1,000 card balance

Why does my statement interest differ from the table?
Your card most likely uses the daily balance method, the number of days in each cycle varies, and new purchases or payment timing change the average balance. The table is a clean benchmark, not a statement prediction.

Does paying twice a month help?
A little, because it lowers the average daily balance. Paying more in total does far more.

Is 30% APR realistic?
Card rates vary widely by issuer, card type and credit history, and some cards and penalty rates are in that range. The Federal Reserve publishes average card rates in its consumer credit statistics; your exact APR is on your statement.

Will paying the minimum hurt my credit?
Paying at least the minimum on time keeps the account current. A high balance relative to your limit, however, can weigh on credit scores until it is paid down.

Try it with your numbers: enter your real balance, APR and payment in the Credit Card Payoff calculator to see your own months and total interest.

Sources

  • Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: Credit cards
  • Federal Reserve Board

Every table figure was simulated month by month (interest = balance x APR / 12, rounded to the cent, then the payment applied). Last reviewed: November 2026. This is general information about how card interest works, not advice on any specific card; your cardholder agreement governs your rates, fees and grace period.

title: Overtime Pay on a 4x10 Schedule: How the Federal 40-Hour Rule Works
meta: A 4x10 week of 40 hours earns no federal overtime. At $24/hour, a 10-hour fifth day makes the week pay $1,320. Plus California's daily OT rule.
html:
Under federal law, overtime is owed for hours worked over 40 in a workweek, not for hours over 8 in a day. So a standard 4x10 schedule (four 10-hour days, 40 hours) earns no federal overtime, even though each day runs 2 hours past the usual 8.

Overtime starts only when the week goes past 40, for example if you pick up a fifth day. Some states, most notably California, add daily overtime rules on top of the federal one.

The federal rule, piece by piece

The Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) sets the federal baseline for most private and public employers:

  • Threshold: covered, non-exempt employees must get overtime for hours worked over 40 in a workweek.
  • Rate: at least one and one-half times the employee's regular rate of pay. At $24 an hour that is $36.
  • Workweek: a fixed, recurring period of 168 hours, seven consecutive 24-hour periods. It can start on any day and at any hour your employer sets, but it cannot be changed week to week to avoid overtime.
  • No averaging: each workweek stands alone. A 50-hour week followed by a 30-hour week still owes 10 hours of overtime for the first week.
  • No daily or weekend rule: federal law does not require overtime just because you worked a long day, a Saturday, a Sunday or a holiday, unless those hours push the week past 40.

Certain bonuses and shift differentials can raise the regular rate above your base wage. The examples below assume a flat $24 an hour.

Worked pay table: a 4x10 worker at $24 an hour

Regular hours are paid at $24 and overtime hours at $36. Only hours worked count toward the 40.

WeekDaily hoursHours workedRegular hoursOT hoursGross pay
Standard 4x1010, 10, 10, 1040400$960
4x10 plus a 5-hour Friday10, 10, 10, 10, 545405$1,140
4x10 plus a 10-hour Friday10, 10, 10, 10, 10504010$1,320
One 12-hour day in a 4x10 week12, 10, 10, 1042402$1,032
Unpaid day off, then a 10-hour Friday10, off, 10, 10, 1040400$960
Paid holiday (10 h) plus 4 worked days of 10Holiday, 10, 10, 10, 1040 (+10 paid holiday)400$1,200

How to read it:

  • The standard 4x10 pays $960, exactly the same as 40 hours spread over five 8-hour days.
  • A 10-hour fifth day adds 10 overtime hours: 40 x $24 = $960, plus 10 x $36 = $360, for $1,320.
  • A single 12-hour day does not trigger overtime by itself. It counts only because it brings the week to 42 hours, so 2 hours are paid at $36.
  • Paid holiday hours are generally not "hours worked" for federal overtime. In the last row you worked 40 hours and were paid 10 more for the holiday at straight time, for $1,200. Some employers choose to count holiday or PTO hours toward overtime, so check your policy.

To total a week of clock-in and clock-out times before you check your pay stub, use the Hours calculator.

States with daily overtime: the California example

States can set stricter rules than the FLSA, and when both apply, the employee gets whichever standard is more generous. California is the best-known example of daily overtime. It generally requires time and a half for hours over 8 in a workday and double time for hours over 12 in a workday, in addition to a weekly 40-hour rule.

Under that daily rule, a plain 4x10 week would include 2 overtime hours each day: 32 regular hours x $24 = $768 plus 8 overtime hours x $36 = $288, for $1,056 instead of $960. That is why California employers who use 10-hour days typically adopt an alternative workweek schedule, which must be approved through a secret-ballot vote of the affected employees and allows up to 10 hours a day at straight time within a 40-hour week. A few other states also have daily overtime rules, so check your state labor department.

Exempt or non-exempt: does the rule apply to you?

The overtime rule covers non-exempt employees, which includes most hourly workers. Exempt employees are not owed overtime, but being on a salary does not make you exempt by itself. To be exempt under the common executive, administrative and professional exemptions, a job generally has to pass three tests:

  • Salary basis: paid a predetermined salary that is not cut for variations in the quality or quantity of work.
  • Salary level: paid at least the minimum weekly amount set in federal regulations. That figure has changed and been challenged in court, so check the Department of Labor for the current number.
  • Duties: the actual job duties meet the exemption's definition. A job title alone does not decide it.

If you are salaried and non-exempt, overtime still applies, calculated from your regular rate. To see what an hourly rate or a salary offer comes to over a year, use the Hourly to Salary calculator.

4x10 overtime questions, answered

Can my employer make me work a 4x10 without overtime?
Under federal law, yes, as long as the week totals 40 hours or less. Daily overtime only comes from state law, where it exists.

What if I work 9 hours one day and 11 the next?
Federally, only the weekly total matters. Four days of 9, 11, 10 and 10 is 40 hours with no overtime.

Does a 4x10 change if my workweek starts on Wednesday?
It can. Overtime is measured inside your employer's defined workweek, so an extra shift is counted in whichever workweek it falls.

Can I take comp time instead of overtime pay?
Private employers generally cannot replace overtime pay with comp time under the FLSA. Public sector employers have separate rules.

Try it with your numbers: add up your actual shifts with the Hours calculator, then see the yearly effect of your rate with the Hourly to Salary calculator.

Sources

  • U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division: Overtime Pay
  • U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division: Minimum Wage

Every pay figure was computed as regular hours x $24 plus overtime hours x $36. Last reviewed: November 2026. This is general information about federal overtime rules, not legal advice; your state law, union contract or employer policy may give you more.

title: Why Your Mortgage Escrow Payment Went Up and How to Check It
meta: A $900 rise in tax and insurance can lift escrow from $500 to $662.50 a month. How the escrow analysis, two-month cushion cap and shortage work.
html:
Your mortgage escrow payment usually goes up for two reasons, often at the same time: your property tax or homeowners insurance bill rose, so the servicer has to collect more each month, and the account came up short last year, so you are also repaying the gap. Both show up after the servicer's annual escrow analysis.

In the example below, a $900 jump in tax and insurance turns a $500 monthly escrow payment into $662.50 for the next year, and $575 after that.

What happens at the annual escrow analysis

If your loan has an escrow account, your servicer collects part of each payment and pays the tax and insurance bills for you. At least once a year it reviews the account and sends you an escrow statement. The process goes like this:

  1. Look back: it compares what it collected with what it actually paid out for taxes and insurance over the past year.
  2. Look ahead: it estimates the coming year's bills, usually based on the most recent ones, and when each is due.
  3. Set the cushion: federal rules under the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA) let the servicer keep a cushion of up to one-sixth of the estimated annual disbursements, about two months' worth. Your loan documents or state law may allow less.
  4. Find the gap: it projects the account month by month and checks whether the lowest point would dip below the cushion. If it would, there is a shortage. If the account would hold more than needed, there is a surplus.

Shortage, deficiency and surplus are different things

TermWhat it meansHow repayment usually works
ShortageThe account is projected to fall below its target balance for the year ahead.If it is at least one month's escrow payment, the servicer can let it stand or spread it over at least 12 monthly payments. If it is smaller, it may ask for it within 30 days or spread it out.
DeficiencyThe account actually went negative because the servicer advanced money to pay a bill.A small deficiency may be due within 30 days; a larger one is generally repaid in two or more monthly installments.
SurplusThe account holds more than it needs.Generally refunded if it is $50 or more and your loan is current; smaller amounts may be credited to next year.

These are the general federal rules for most escrowed mortgages; your statement says which applies and what options you have.

Worked example: tax and insurance both go up

Say last year's escrow was built around a $4,200 property tax bill and a $1,800 insurance premium. This year the servicer paid a $4,500 tax bill and a $2,400 renewal premium out of the account, and it expects the same bills next year.

ItemLast yearThis yearChange
Property tax$4,200$4,500+$300 (7.1%)
Homeowners insurance$1,800$2,400+$600 (33.3%)
Total annual bills$6,000$6,900+$900
Base escrow payment (bills / 12)$500$575+$75
Maximum cushion (bills / 6)$1,000$1,150+$150

Now the shortage. Last year the account paid out $900 more than it was built to collect, and the allowed cushion grew by $150. In a simplified version where the bills come due at the same times each year, that leaves a shortage of about $900 + $150 = $1,050. A real analysis projects every month, so the timing of your tax installments can push the actual figure up or down.

  • Spread over 12 months: $1,050 / 12 = $87.50 a month. New escrow payment: $575 + $87.50 = $662.50, up $162.50 (32.5%) from $500.
  • Paid as a lump sum: $1,050 now, and the escrow payment rises only to $575.
  • The following year: once the shortage is repaid, the payment drops back to about $575, assuming the bills stay the same.

Principal and interest on a fixed-rate loan do not change, so the whole increase is escrow. To see how a new tax or insurance figure changes the full monthly payment, enter it in the Mortgage calculator.

A checklist before you accept the new payment

  • Match the tax figure to your tax bill. Look up your bill on your county or city site and compare it with the amount on the escrow statement. Check that any exemption you qualify for, such as a homestead exemption where offered, has been applied.
  • Look at your assessment. If it jumped, find your local appeal process and deadline.
  • Shop the insurance. Get quotes with similar coverage. If you switch, send the new declarations page to your servicer so it pays the right insurer and amount.
  • Watch for force-placed insurance. If the servicer believes your policy lapsed, it may buy coverage that usually costs far more. A big unexplained insurance jump is worth a call.
  • Ask for a new analysis after a change. If your tax bill is lowered on appeal or you find cheaper insurance, ask the servicer to rerun the analysis. Servicers can often do this, which may lower the payment before next year.
  • Dispute errors in writing. If the numbers look wrong, send a written notice of error to the address your servicer lists for that purpose.

If you are shopping for a home, build realistic tax and insurance figures into your budget from the start. The Home Affordability calculator shows how those costs change the price you can afford.

Escrow questions homeowners often have

Why did my payment go up if my interest rate is fixed?
A fixed rate locks principal and interest, not taxes and insurance. Escrow follows those bills, so the total payment can rise even on a fixed-rate loan.

Can I get rid of escrow?
Sometimes. Some lenders allow you to waive escrow after you build enough equity, sometimes for a fee, while some loans, including many government-backed ones, generally require it. Ask your servicer.

Should I pay the shortage in a lump sum?
It keeps the monthly payment at the base amount. Spreading it out is fine if you would rather keep the cash; your statement lists the options your servicer offers.

Try it with your numbers: put your new tax and insurance amounts into the Mortgage calculator to see your full monthly payment.

Sources

  • Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: Mortgages
  • Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: Buying a house
  • U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)

All example figures were worked out step by step (bills / 12, bills / 6, shortage / 12). Last reviewed: November 2026. This is general information about escrow accounts; your servicer's escrow statement and loan documents control your actual payment, so contact your servicer with questions about your account.
